title: Drug-induced blistering (SJS/TEN, FDE, AGEP)
summary: Drugs cause a range of blistering reactions, from a single recurring fixed drug eruption to SJS/TEN, which is a medical emergency. Stop the culprit early, record the allergy and report on a Yellow Card.

glance.think: Blistering, dusky or pustular rash 4–28 days after starting a drug (days for AGEP; hours for repeat fixed drug eruption).
glance.engine: T-cell-mediated keratinocyte death (SJS/TEN, FDE), neutrophilic reactions (AGEP) or drug-triggered autoantibodies (linear IgA, pemphigoid, pemphigus).
glance.backbone: Identify and stop the culprit, admit SJS/TEN, document the allergy clearly, Yellow Card, and screen high-risk drugs (HLA-B*1502 before carbamazepine in at-risk groups).
glance.never_miss: SJS/TEN: skin pain, fever, mucosal erosions and Nikolsky-positive skin detachment.

what: This is a group of reactions in which a drug causes vesicles, bullae, pustules or epidermal necrosis. They range from trivial (localised FDE) to life-threatening (TEN). For the IP, **drug causation** is the main reason to know them.

rows: ACD to topicals (neomycin, fragrance), systemic contact dermatitis
T-cell/IL-8/neutrophils. **Hours to 2 days** (short latency). Hundreds of non-follicular pustules on erythema, flexural first, with fever and neutrophilia; resolves within ~2 weeks of stopping
Resident CD8 T cells. Recurs at the **same site** (lips, genitals, hands) within ~30 min to 8 h of re-exposure; heals with violaceous-brown pigmentation
**Allopurinol**, **carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin, phenobarbital**, **sulfonamides (co-trimoxazole)**, sulfasalazine, NSAIDs (oxicams), nevirapine

Cytotoxic T cells, granulysin, Fas-FasL. Latency **4–28 days** (lamotrigine risk is higher with fast titration or valproate). HLA-B*15:02 (carbamazepine; South-East Asian ancestry) and HLA-B*58:01 (allopurinol). EM is usually HSV-related, not drug-related (see the [inflammatory rash pages](condition:erythema-multiforme) notes)
**Thiols: penicillamine, captopril**; ACE inhibitors, rifampicin, piroxicam
Often foliaceus-like and remits on stopping (more with thiols)
**DPP-4 inhibitors (gliptins)**, loop diuretics, spironolactone, PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors, penicillins, etanercept (case reports)
Months to years of latency for gliptins
**Vancomycin** (classic), penicillins, cephalosporins, captopril, NSAIDs, amiodarone, lithium
Within days; annular "string of pearls" and haemorrhagic/TEN-like forms possible
**Naproxen**, other NSAIDs, tetracyclines, furosemide, nalidixic acid, isotretinoin; sunbeds; dialysis

features: **SJS/TEN** classification by detached BSA: **SJS <10%**, **SJS/TEN overlap 10–30%**, **TEN >30%** (**Module 4 exam Q27**, 40% = TEN).

list: Prodrome: fever, sore throat and eye symptoms 1–3 days before the skin.
Then **painful** dusky macules or atypical flat targets, which form bullae and sheet-like detachment with a positive Nikolsky sign.
**≥2 mucosal sites** are involved (oral haemorrhagic crusting of the lips, conjunctivitis, genital; photo E02).

features: **SSSS** is the toxin-mediated mimic in young children: superficial peeling, mucosa **spared**, and the child is irritable and tender.
diagnosis: Diagnosis is mostly clinical, with urgent specialist confirmation and frozen-section or standard biopsy. **SCORTEN** (calculated in the first 24 h) predicts mortality. Its 7 points are:
For drug causation use **ALDEN** (for SJS/TEN). Patch testing is useful later for FDE and AGEP. For DRESS (the systemic DDx), RegiSCAR.

list: DRESS (facial oedema, eosinophilia, organ involvement, latency 2–8 weeks)

**Suspected SJS/TEN or extensive or mucosal blistering:** **STOP all non-essential drugs immediately**, especially the likely culprits started 4–28 days ago; **999 / same-day ED** for transfer to a **burns or dermatology intensive unit** (UK SJS/TEN guideline, Creamer 2016). Don't wait for a GP appointment; **Ophthalmology within 24 h**, and urology/gynaecology/oral medicine input; Specialist adjuncts: ciclosporin, IVIG (the evidence for blocking Fas-FasL is mixed and UK guidance does not routinely recommend it), steroids, and anti-TNF (etanercept, being studied)
**AGEP:** stop the drug, give supportive care and a potent TCS. Refer the same day if febrile or extensive.
**FDE:** stop and avoid the culprit; a potent TCS for 1–2 weeks; document the specific drug.
**Drug-induced BP or pemphigus:** stop the culprit and follow the specialist pathway. Recovery may take months.

**Allergy documentation:** Record the exact drug and reaction in the GP record (SNOMED) and on the patient's allergy list; **Report to MHRA Yellow Card** (all serious reactions; anything involving a black-triangle drug); For SJS/TEN: lifelong avoidance of the culprit and **structurally related drugs**, and **advice for first-degree relatives** about HLA risk. A MedicAlert bracelet is reasonable

**Prevention (pharmacist role):** **HLA-B*15:02** screening before carbamazepine in people of Han Chinese or Thai ancestry (BNF/MHRA); Start allopurinol low (100 mg) and titrate in CKD; Follow the **lamotrigine** titration schedule (halve doses with valproate), and counsel all new starters to **stop and seek help with any rash, fever or mouth ulcers in the first 8 weeks**

red_flags: **Skin pain, fever, dusky targets, mucosal erosions or skin detachment**: SJS/TEN, stop all non-essential drugs and call 999 / admit (burns unit or ICU).
Widespread sterile pustules with fever after a new drug (AGEP): same-day assessment.
Rash with fever, facial swelling, lymph nodes and abnormal liver tests: **DRESS**.
pearls: Ask **"What new medicine did you start in the last 8 weeks?"** at every acute rash with fever, skin pain or mucosal involvement.
**Skin pain out of proportion + mucosal erosions + dusky skin = SJS/TEN** until proven otherwise.
Paracetamol can cause FDE, so don't assume over-the-counter means innocent. Always ask about OTC and herbal products.
